contextNote: Chewang Lepcha of Dzongu, popularly known as the ‘Seed Keeper of Dzongu,’ shares traditional knowledge about Lepcha indigenous crops, seed preservation, and cultivation practices learned from his forefathers. He describes nature-based signs, including the appearance and calls of particular birds, used to guide sowing times. He explains the connection between indigenous crops such as millet and foxtail millet, Lepcha rituals and traditions, and the community's relationship with nature.

contextNote: This is the folklore behind the name of Rey Village in East Sikkim. Nimpincho Lepcha (Bongthing) recounts Mun Nyukung Purmit, a powerful female spiritual practitioner, decided to confront the devil. Devil Pond was once a place of fear and mystery. In ancient times, a devil was believed to abduct animals and young children from the nearby village ( Gangyap west Sikkim India), taking them to the pond and killing them. The villagers lived in fear of this evil presence. Mun Nyukung Purmit, a powerful female spiritual practitioner, decided to confront the devil. Using her spiritual power and sacred abilities, she destroyed the pond and defeated the evil force. Her courage and spiritual strength brought relief to the villagers.
